It's the primary output format for **GFS, HRRR, NBM, GEFS, NAM**, and similar numerical weather prediction products.\n54\t\n55\tDecoding it means handling multi-section message framing, four grid geometries, parameter tables indexed by discipline/category/number, five data-packing algorithms, and bitmaps for missing-value masking.\n56\t\n57\tThe standard tools (`wgrib2`, `eccodes`) are C programs. If you need decoded GRIB2 values in a Rust project, your options were: shell out, bind through FFI, or give up and parse bytes yourself.\n58\t\n59\t**gribtract is the native Rust alternative.**\n60\t\n61\t## ✨ Features\n62\t\n63\t- 🦀 **Pure Rust core** — no C toolchain or FFI for simple, complex, complex+spatial-differencing, and PNG packing (DRT 5.0 / 5.2 / 5.3 / 5.41); JPEG2000 (5.40) available behind the optional `jpeg2000` feature\n64\t- 🏷️ **Typed output** — every decoded field carries structured metadata: parameter ID, level, forecast time, grid geometry\n65\t- 🗺️ **Four grid projections** — lat/lon (GDT 3.0), polar stereographic (3.20), Lambert conformal (3.30), Gaussian (3.40)\n66\t- ⚡ **Lazy decode path** — parse headers only, defer grid data; extract single grid points in **O(1)** for DRT=0 fields without decoding the full grid\n67\t- 📈 **Timeseries extractor** — pull per-station forecast series for a list of lat/lon coordinates in one call\n68\t- 🌐 **Byte-range fetching** — `gribtract-fetch` downloads GRIB2 (or slices of it) from NOAA S3, GCS, and NOMADS over HTTP range requests\n69\t- 🐍 **Python bindings** — `gribtract-py` (PyO3) exposes the decoder to Python\n70\t- ✅ **Oracle-gated correctness** — every release is verified against eccodes/wgrib2 over a corpus of real NOAA files; agreement can only ratchet up\n71\t\n72\t## 🌍 Geographic Coverage\n73\t\n74\tgribtract provides comprehensive coverage for CONUS (Continental United States) weather station data extraction, validated against real NOAA HRRR CONUS GRIB2 files.\n75\t\n76\t### Validated Coverage Areas\n77\t\n78\t**CONUS Coverage:** ✅ **100% station coverage confirmed** (56/56 stations tested)\n79\t\n80\tThe HRRR CONUS grid (Lambert Conformal Conic, 3km resolution) covers:\n81\t- **Northern extent:** 48.57°N (International Falls, MN)\n82\t- **Southern extent:** 25.91°N (Brownsville, TX) \n83\t- **Western extent:** 122.60°W (Portland, OR)\n84\t- **Eastern extent:** 71.01°W (Boston, MA)\n85\t\n86\t### Station Coverage by Region\n87\t\n88\t| Region | Stations | Coverage | Notes |\n89\t|--------|----------|----------|-------|\n90\t| East Coast | 5 | 100% | 4 marginal stations near grid edge |\n91\t| Southeast | 8 | 100% | Florida peninsula covered |\n92\t| Midwest | 8 | 100% | Excellent coverage, no edge issues |\n93\t| South Central | 7 | 100% | Well-covered region |\n94\t| Mountain | 4 | 100% | No coverage gaps |\n95\t| West Coast | 8 | 100% | 7 marginal stations near grid edge |\n96\t| Southwest | 4 | 100% | Good coverage |\n97\t| Northern Border | 6 | 100% | Complete border coverage |\n98\t| Southern Border | 5 | 100% | Complete border coverage |\n99\t\n100\t### Geographic Limitations\n101\t\n102\t⚠️ **Edge Proximity:** ~27% of tested stations are within 100 km of grid boundaries, particularly:\n103\t- **West Coast stations:** Seattle, Portland, San Francisco, Los Angeles (near eastern grid edge)\n104\t- **East Coast stations:** Boston, New York, Philadelphia (near western grid edge)\n105\t- **Florida stations:** Miami, Ft. // JFK\n173\t        if let Some(value) = decode_point_drt0(body, &lf.packing, idx) {\n174\t            println!(\"value at JFK: {value}\");\n175\t        }\n176\t    }\n177\t}\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\t### Extract a forecast timeseries for a list of stations\n181\t\n182\t```rust\n183\tuse gribtract::timeseries::{extract_timeseries, ParameterRecord, Station, TimeseriesRequest};\n184\t\n185\t// 2m temperature (discipline=0, category=0, number=0), height-above-ground level (type=103)\n186\tlet request = TimeseriesRequest {\n187\t    parameter: ParameterRecord { discipline: 0, category: 0, number: 0 },\n188\t    level_type1: 103,\n189\t    stations: vec![\n190\t        Station { id: \"JFK\".into(), lat: 40.64,  lon: -73.78  },\n191\t        Station { id: \"ORD\".into(), lat: 41.979, lon: -87.905 },\n192\t        Station { id: \"LAX\".into(), lat: 33.943, lon: -118.408 },\n193\t    ],\n194\t};\n195\t\n196\tlet fields = gribtract::decode(&bytes)?;\n197\tlet ts = extract_timeseries(&fields, &request);\n198\t\n199\tfor (station, rows) in &ts.stations {\n200\t    println!(\"Station: {station}\");\n201\t    for row in rows {\n202\t        println!(\"  forecast hour {}: {:?}\", row.forecast_hour, row.value);\n203\t    }\n204\t}\n205\t```\n206\t\n207\t### Decode a DRT=3 grid (complex + spatial differencing) — extract many stations\n208\t\n209\tDRT=3 requires a full sequential decode; random access isn't possible. The recommended pattern is **decode once, extract many**:\n210\t\n211\t```rust\n212\tuse gribtract::{decode_lazy, decode_all_drt3};\n213\t\n214\tlet lazy_fields = gribtract::decode_lazy(&bytes)?;\n215\tfor lf in &lazy_fields {\n216\t    if let (Some(body), Some(extra)) = (&lf.section7_raw, &lf.complex_extra) {\n217\t        let n = lf.grid.num_data_points as usize;\n218\t        let grid: Vec<f64> = decode_all_drt3(body, &lf.packing, extra, n)?;\n219\t\n220\t        // Now extract any number of stations by index, O(1) each\n221\t        for (lat, lon) in &station_coords {\n222\t            let idx = lf.grid.nearest_index(*lat, *lon)?;\n223\t            println!(\"value: {}\", grid[idx]);\n224\t        }\n225\t    }\n226\t}\n227\t```\n228\t\n229\t### 🐍 Python\n230\t\n231\t```bash\n232\tpip install maturin\n233\tmaturin develop -p gribtract-py\n234\t```\n235\t\n236\t```python\n237\timport gribtract\n238\t\n239\tfields = gribtract.decode(open(\"hrrr.t00z.wrfsfcf01.grib2\", \"rb\").read())\n240\tfor f in fields:\n241\t    print(f.parameter, f.level, f.forecast_hour)\n242\t```\n243\t\n244\t## 🔬 The Correctness Oracle\n245\t\n246\tgribtract is built **oracle-first**: correctness is defined as agreement with eccodes/wgrib2 over real files, not as passing hand-written unit tests.\n247\t\n248\t```\n249\tgribtract decode  ─┐\n250\t                   ├─→ compare field-by-field + grid values within derived tolerance\n251\teccodes/wgrib2    ─┘\n252\t```\n253\t\n254\tThe differential harness in `gribtract-testutil` runs both decoders over a corpus of real NOAA GRIB2 files (GFS, HRRR, NBM, GEFS) and compares:\n255\t\n256\t- **Metadata exactly** — center, parameter ID, level, forecast time, grid geometry\n257\t- **Grid values within derived tolerance** — computed from the packing template's own scale factors, never an arbitrary epsilon\n258\t\n259\tAny disagreement becomes a permanent regression fixture. The agreement percentage can only increase; there is no mechanism to silently drop a covered template.\n260\t\n261\t```bash\n262\t# Run the differential tests\n263\tcargo test -p gribtract -- differential\n264\t\n265\t# Fetch and verify against the full corpus (requires eccodes installed)\n266\tcargo xtask corpus fetch\n267\tcargo xtask corpus verify\n268\t```\n269\t\n270\t## 📊 Performance Dashboard\n271\t\n272\tA self-contained benchmark dashboard (`dashboard.html`) tracks decode throughput on real NOAA files, fed by `bench-results.json`. Speed numbers are never reported without a corresponding correctness verification run.\n273\t\n274\t```bash\n275\tcargo xtask bench    # run benchmarks, regenerate bench-results.json\n276\tcargo xtask serve    # serve the live dashboard with streaming updates\n277\t```\n278\t\n279\t## 🏗️ Building from Source\n280\t\n281\tRequires **Rust 1.75+**.\n282\t\n283\t```bash\n284\tgit clone https://github.com/jedarden/gribtract\n285\tcd gribtract\n286\tcargo build --release\n287\t```\n288\t\n289\tThe `gribtract-py` extension is excluded from the default workspace build (it needs Python headers for PyO3) — build it explicitly with `maturin develop -p gribtract-py`.\n290\t\n291\t## 💻 CLI Reference\n292\t\n293\t```bash\n294\tgribtract list   forecast.grib2   # 📋 list all fields (JSON)\n295\tgribtract decode forecast.grib2   # 📤 decode all fields + values (JSON)\n296\tgribtract dump   forecast.grib2   # 🔍 raw hex dump\n297\t```\n298\t\n299\tThe CLI is intended as a thin wrapper over the library API for ad-hoc inspection.\n300\t\n301\t## 📜 License\n302\t\n303\tMIT OR Apache-2.0, at your option.\n304\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"1444215e-abc1-4c91-9094-65d891e18d2a","uuid":"838f4710-14d8-4b02-b1d0-d1c552b1ef3c","timestamp":"2026-07-24T09:33:08.860Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/home/coding/gribtract/README.md","content":"# 🌦️ gribtract\n\n**A pure-Rust GRIB2 decoder** — turn NOAA/WMO weather model output into typed fields and gridded numbers, verified field-by-field against eccodes/wgrib2.\n\n![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue.svg)\n![Rust 1.75+](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.75%2B-orange.svg)\n\nNo C toolchain. No I/O.\n│   ├── gribtract           # 📚 High-level API: message iterator, field selection, timeseries\n│   ├── gribtract-cli       # 💻 `gribtract decode|list|dump` command-line tool\n│   ├── gribtract-fetch     # 🌐 HTTP byte-range fetching from S3 / GCS / NOMADS\n│   ├── gribtract-py        # 🐍 Python bindings via PyO3 (excluded from default build)\n│   └── gribtract-testutil  # 🧪 Differential harness: corpus, golden fixtures, diff\n└── xtask                   # 🛠️ Corpus management, reference-decoder runner, bench dashboard\n```\n\n`gribtract-core` is the zero-dependency parsing core. `gribtract` is the crate you depend on for library use. `gribtract-cli` builds the standalone `gribtract` binary.\n\n## 📖 Usage\n\n### Decode all fields from a GRIB2 file\n\n```rust\nuse gribtract::{decode, Field};\n\nlet bytes = std::fs::read(\"hrrr.t00z.wrfsfcf01.grib2\")?;\nlet fields: Vec<Field> = gribtract::decode(&bytes)?;\n\nfor field in &fields {\n    println!(\n        \"param={}/{}/{}  level={}  forecast_offset={}h\",\n        field.parameter.discipline,\n        field.parameter.category,\n        field.parameter.number,\n        field.level.value1(),\n        field.forecast_time.offset_seconds() / 3600,\n    );\n}\n```\n\n### Extract a single grid point — O(1), no full decode\n\n```rust\nuse gribtract::{decode_lazy, decode_point_drt0};\n\nlet fields = gribtract::decode_lazy(&bytes)?;\nfor lf in &fields {\n    if let Some(body) = &lf.section7_raw {\n        let idx = lf.grid.nearest_index(40.64, -73.78)?; // JFK\n        if let Some(value) = decode_point_drt0(body, &lf.packing, idx) {\n            println!(\"value at JFK: {value}\");\n        }\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Extract a forecast timeseries for a list of stations\n\n```rust\nuse gribtract::timeseries::{extract_timeseries, ParameterRecord, Station, TimeseriesRequest};\n\n// 2m temperature (discipline=0, category=0, number=0), height-above-ground level (type=103)\nlet request = TimeseriesRequest {\n    parameter: ParameterRecord { discipline: 0, category: 0, number: 0 },\n    level_type1: 103,\n    stations: vec![\n        Station { id: \"JFK\".into(), lat: 40.64,  lon: -73.78  },\n        Station { id: \"ORD\".into(), lat: 41.979, lon: -87.905 },\n        Station { id: \"LAX\".into(), lat: 33.943, lon: -118.408 },\n    ],\n};\n\nlet fields = gribtract::decode(&bytes)?;\nlet ts = extract_timeseries(&fields, &request);\n\nfor (station, rows) in &ts.stations {\n    println!(\"Station: {station}\");\n    for row in rows {\n        println!(\"  forecast hour {}: {:?}\", row.forecast_hour, row.value);\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Decode a DRT=3 grid (complex + spatial differencing) — extract many stations\n\nDRT=3 requires a full sequential decode; random access isn't possible. The recommended pattern is **decode once, extract many**:\n\n```rust\nuse gribtract::{decode_lazy, decode_all_drt3};\n\nlet lazy_fields = gribtract::decode_lazy(&bytes)?;\nfor lf in &lazy_fields {\n    if let (Some(body), Some(extra)) = (&lf.section7_raw, &lf.complex_extra) {\n        let n = lf.grid.num_data_points as usize;\n        let grid: Vec<f64> = decode_all_drt3(body, &lf.packing, extra, n)?;\n\n        // Now extract any number of stations by index, O(1) each\n        for (lat, lon) in &station_coords {\n            let idx = lf.grid.nearest_index(*lat, *lon)?;\n            println!(\"value: {}\", grid[idx]);\n        }\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### 🐍 Python\n\n```bash\npip install maturin\nmaturin develop -p gribtract-py\n```\n\n```python\nimport gribtract\n\nfields = gribtract.decode(open(\"hrrr.t00z.wrfsfcf01.grib2\", \"rb\").read())\nfor f in fields:\n    print(f.parameter, f.level, f.forecast_hour)\n```\n\n## 🔬 The Correctness Oracle\n\ngribtract is built **oracle-first**: correctness is defined as agreement with eccodes/wgrib2 over real files, not as passing hand-written unit tests.\n\n```\ngribtract decode  ─┐\n                   ├─→ compare field-by-field + grid values within derived tolerance\neccodes/wgrib2    ─┘\n```\n\nThe differential harness in `gribtract-testutil` runs both decoders over a corpus of real NOAA GRIB2 files (GFS, HRRR, NBM, GEFS) and compares:\n\n- **Metadata exactly** — center, parameter ID, level, forecast time, grid geometry\n- **Grid values within derived tolerance** — computed from the packing template's own scale factors, never an arbitrary epsilon\n\nAny disagreement becomes a permanent regression fixture. The agreement percentage can only increase; there is no mechanism to silently drop a covered template.\n\n```bash\n# Run the differential tests\ncargo test -p gribtract -- differential\n\n# Fetch and verify against the full corpus (requires eccodes installed)\ncargo xtask corpus fetch\ncargo xtask corpus verify\n```\n\n## 📊 Performance Dashboard\n\nA self-contained benchmark dashboard (`dashboard.html`) tracks decode throughput on real NOAA files, fed by `bench-results.json`. Speed numbers are never reported without a corresponding correctness verification run.\n\n```bash\ncargo xtask bench    # run benchmarks, regenerate bench-results.json\ncargo xtask serve    # serve the live dashboard with streaming updates\n```\n\n## 🏗️ Building from Source\n\nRequires **Rust 1.75+**.\n\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/jedarden/gribtract\ncd gribtract\ncargo build --release\n```\n\nThe `gribtract-py` extension is excluded from the default workspace build (it needs Python headers for PyO3) — build it explicitly with `maturin develop -p gribtract-py`.\n\n## 💻 CLI Reference\n\n```bash\ngribtract list   forecast.grib2   # 📋 list all fields (JSON)\ngribtract decode forecast.grib2   # 📤 decode all fields + values (JSON)\ngribtract dump   forecast.grib2   # 🔍 raw hex dump\n```\n\nThe CLI is intended as a thin wrapper over the library API for ad-hoc inspection.\n\n## 📜 License\n\nMIT OR Apache-2.0, at your option.\n","numLines":304,"startLine":1,"totalLines":304}}}

Appendix\n\n### Grid Template 0 Specification\n\n**Definition:** Regular Latitude-Longitude Grid (WMO GRIB2 Grid Definition Template 0)\n\n**Characteristics:**\n- **Shape:** Earth represented as regular lat/lon grid\n- **Projection:** Geographic (no projection distortion)\n- **Spacing:** Uniform in both latitude and longitude\n- **Extent:** Global (90°N to -90°N, 0°E to 359.75°E for GFS)\n\n**Parameters:**\n- `Ni`: Number of points along latitude circle (varies by resolution)\n- `Nj`: Number of points along longitude meridian (varies by resolution)\n- `Di`: Longitudinal direction increment (varies by resolution)\n- `Dj`: Latitudinal direction increment (varies by resolution)\n\n**CONUS Compatibility:**\n- CONUS bounds (20°N-50°N, 125°W-65°W) are subset of global grid\n- No interpolation or projection issues over CONUS\n- Uniform resolution across CONUS without edge effects\n\n### File Naming Convention\n\n**Pattern:** `gfs.YYYYMMDD/HH/atmos/gfs.tHHz.pgrb2.RESOLUTION.FFH`\n\n**Components:**\n- `gfs`: Model identifier (Global Forecast System)\n- `YYYYMMDD`: Model run date (e.g., 20260724)\n- `HH`: Cycle hour (00, 06, 12, 18)\n- `atmos`: Atmospheric model (vs. ocean/wave)\n- `tHHz`: Forecast cycle (e.g., t00z for 00Z cycle)\n- `pgrb2`: Product GRIB2 format\n- `RESOLUTION`: Grid spacing (0p25=0.25°, 0p50=0.50°, 1p00=1.00°)\n- `FFH`: Forecast hour (000=analysis, 003=3-hour, ..., 384=16-day)\n\n**Example:** `gfs.20260724/00/atmos/gfs.t00z.pgrb2.0p50.f000`\n- GFS model from 2026-07-24 00Z cycle\n- 0.50° resolution\n- F000 = analysis time (0-hour forecast)\n\n### Download Performance Formula\n\n**Calculation:**\n```\nDownload Time (seconds) = File Size (bytes) / (Connection Speed (bps) × 60 seconds)\n\nConnection Speeds:\n- 100 Mbps = 12.5 MB/s = 100,000,000 bps\n- 10 Mbps = 1.25 MB/s = 10,000,000 bps  \n- 1 Mbps = 0.125 MB/s = 1,000,000 bps\n```\n\n**Examples:**\n- 145 MB @ 100 Mbps: 145 MB / 12.5 MB/s = 11.6 seconds\n- 145 MB @ 10 Mbps: 145 MB / 1.25 MB/s = 116 seconds (1:56)\n- 490 MB @ 100 Mbps: 490 MB / 12.5 MB/s = 39.2 seconds\n\n### Related Documentation\n\n**Project Appendix\n\n### Grid Template 0 Specification\n\n**Definition:** Regular Latitude-Longitude Grid (WMO GRIB2 Grid Definition Template 0)\n\n**Characteristics:**\n- **Shape:** Earth represented as regular lat/lon grid\n- **Projection:** Geographic (no projection distortion)\n- **Spacing:** Uniform in both latitude and longitude\n- **Extent:** Global (90°N to -90°N, 0°E to 359.75°E for GFS)\n\n**Parameters:**\n- `Ni`: Number of points along latitude circle (varies by resolution)\n- `Nj`: Number of points along longitude meridian (varies by resolution)\n- `Di`: Longitudinal direction increment (varies by resolution)\n- `Dj`: Latitudinal direction increment (varies by resolution)\n\n**CONUS Compatibility:**\n- CONUS bounds (20°N-50°N, 125°W-65°W) are subset of global grid\n- No interpolation or projection issues over CONUS\n- Uniform resolution across CONUS without edge effects\n\n### File Naming Convention\n\n**Pattern:** `gfs.YYYYMMDD/HH/atmos/gfs.tHHz.pgrb2.RESOLUTION.FFH`\n\n**Components:**\n- `gfs`: Model identifier (Global Forecast System)\n- `YYYYMMDD`: Model run date (e.g., 20260724)\n- `HH`: Cycle hour (00, 06, 12, 18)\n- `atmos`: Atmospheric model (vs. ocean/wave)\n- `tHHz`: Forecast cycle (e.g., t00z for 00Z cycle)\n- `pgrb2`: Product GRIB2 format\n- `RESOLUTION`: Grid spacing (0p25=0.25°, 0p50=0.50°, 1p00=1.00°)\n- `FFH`: Forecast hour (000=analysis, 003=3-hour, ..., 384=16-day)\n\n**Example:** `gfs.20260724/00/atmos/gfs.t00z.pgrb2.0p50.f000`\n- GFS model from 2026-07-24 00Z cycle\n- 0.50° resolution\n- F000 = analysis time (0-hour forecast)\n\n### Download Performance Formula\n\n**Calculation:**\n```\nDownload Time (seconds) = File Size (bytes) / (Connection Speed (bps) × 60 seconds)\n\nConnection Speeds:\n- 100 Mbps = 12.5 MB/s = 100,000,000 bps\n- 10 Mbps = 1.25 MB/s = 10,000,000 bps  \n- 1 Mbps = 0.125 MB/s = 1,000,000 bps\n```\n\n**Examples:**\n- 145 MB @ 100 Mbps: 145 MB / 12.5 MB/s = 11.6 seconds\n- 145 MB @ 10 Mbps: 145 MB / 1.25 MB/s = 116 seconds (1:56)\n- 490 MB @ 100 Mbps: 490 MB / 12.5 MB/s = 39.2 seconds\n\n### Related Documentation\n\n**Project
